question: How is a bone fracture best defined in a clinical setting?

options.A: A complete stretching of the muscle ligaments surrounding a joint
options.B: A break or disruption in the structural continuity of a bone
options.C: An infection residing strictly within the bone marrow cavity
options.D: A permanent dislocation of two articulating bone surfaces

explanation: A fracture is defined clinically as a break or disruption in the structural continuity of a bone, which often involves damage to surrounding soft tissues and blood vessels. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h1)

question: Besides the bone itself, what other structures are frequently damaged when a fracture occurs?

options.A: Only the epidermis and superficial hair follicles
options.B: Surrounding soft tissues, blood vessels, nerves, and periosteum
options.C: Strictly the major salivary glands and regional lymph nodes
options.D: Only the articular cartilage within distant joint spaces

explanation: When a bone breaks, the impact forces typically cause concurrent damage to the surrounding soft tissues, blood vessels, nerves, and periosteum. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h1)

question: What occurs during the initial hematoma formation phase of bone healing?

options.A: Osteoclasts dissolve the entire diaphysis of the affected bone
options.B: Bleeding from the bone ends and periosteum creates a blood clot at the site
options.C: Compact bone instantly replaces all cartilaginous structures
options.D: The patient experiences complete loss of all local inflammatory responses

explanation: Immediately following a fracture, bleeding from the broken bone ends and damaged periosteum forms a hematoma within the fracture site. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h2)

question: Which cells are primarily responsible for laying down new compact bone along lines of stress during the remodeling phase?
explanation: Osteoblasts are responsible for laying down new bone tissue, working alongside osteoclasts which resorb excess bone during the remodeling phase. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary difference between a closed fracture and an open fracture?

options.A: Open fractures always involve multiple bone fragments while closed fractures do not
options.B: Closed fractures leave the overlying skin intact, whereas open fractures involve a break in the skin
options.C: Closed fractures occur only in children, whereas open fractures occur exclusively in the elderly
options.D: Open fractures never require surgical intervention, unlike closed fractures

explanation: A closed fracture leaves the skin intact, while an open fracture breaks the skin, exposing the bone and raising infection risks. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h3)

question: Why are greenstick fractures frequently observed in pediatric patients?

options.A: Because children have completely mineralized and rigid cortical bone
options.B: Because children's bones are softer and more pliable, resulting in incomplete breaks
options.C: Because pediatric bones lack any form of periosteum protection
options.D: Because children experience much higher-velocity motor vehicle accidents

explanation: Greenstick fractures are incomplete breaks commonly seen in children because their growing bones are softer and more pliable. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h3)

question: What defines a pathological fracture?

options.A: A fracture caused exclusively by high-speed motor vehicle accidents
options.B: A break occurring in a bone weakened by an underlying disease process
options.C: A fracture that heals completely without any medical intervention
options.D: A break that happens strictly due to repetitive athletic training

explanation: Pathological fractures occur in bones that have been weakened by underlying diseases such as osteoporosis, tumors, or infections. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h4)

question: What is a primary cause of stress or fatigue fractures?

options.B: Repeated, prolonged micro-trauma to the bone over time
options.C: Severe systemic bacterial infections of the bone marrow
options.D: Congenital absence of calcium during fetal development

explanation: Stress or fatigue fractures are caused by repeated, prolonged micro-trauma from activities like intense athletics or heavy labor. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h4)

question: Why should nurses avoid purposely eliciting crepitus during a physical examination?

options.A: It permanently cures the fracture prematurely
options.B: It causes unnecessary pain and can lead to further tissue and nerve damage
options.C: It interferes with the sterile field of open wounds

explanation: Eliciting crepitus causes unnecessary patient pain and can worsen injury to surrounding tissues, blood vessels, and nerves. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h5)

question: What is a key clinical indicator of acute compartment syndrome that nurses must watch for?

options.A: Pain that is disproportionate to the injury and unresponsive to analgesics
options.B: Rapid healing of the bone within the first 48 hours
options.C: Complete absence of any localized swelling or bruising
options.D: A drop in body temperature limited strictly to the affected toe

explanation: Severe pain that is out of proportion to the injury and fails to respond to pain medication is a classic warning sign of acute compartment syndrome. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary rule regarding splinting a fracture in an emergency setting?

options.A: Always forcefully straighten the bone before applying any device
options.B: Splint the extremity in the position it is found ('where they lie')
options.C: Remove all clothing and submerge the limb in hot water
options.D: Apply rigid traction weights immediately at the accident scene

explanation: The golden rule of emergency splinting is to 'splint them where they lie' to avoid causing additional trauma to surrounding nerves and blood vessels. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h6)

question: How should an open fracture wound be managed initially at the scene?

options.A: Push all protruding bone fragments back beneath the skin immediately
options.B: Cover the wound with a clean or sterile dressing without manipulating bone ends
options.C: Apply heavy pressure directly onto the exposed bone to stop growth
options.D: Leave the wound completely uncovered to allow open-air drying

explanation: Open wounds should be covered with clean or sterile dressings to prevent infection, and protruding bone ends must not be pushed back inside. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)?

options.A: To keep the fracture completely immobilized using external plaster bandages only
options.B: To surgically align bone fragments and secure them using internal hardware like plates and screws
options.C: To dissolve the bone ends so they can fuse without any structural support
options.D: To permanently eliminate the need for any postoperative nursing assessments

explanation: ORIF is a surgical procedure that aligns bone fragments directly and holds them securely in place using internal devices such as plates, screws, and nails. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h7)

question: What is a critical nursing responsibility when caring for a patient with a newly applied plaster cast?

options.A: Pour water directly inside the cast daily to keep the skin hydrated
options.B: Monitor for cast tightness and perform frequent neurovascular assessments
options.C: Encourage the patient to insert sharp knitting needles to scratch inner itches
options.D: Remove the cast after 24 hours regardless of healing progress

explanation: Nurses must closely monitor cast tightness and perform regular neurovascular checks to detect signs of impaired circulation or nerve damage early. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h7)

question: What are the classic clinical features of fat embolism syndrome following a long bone fracture?

options.A: Severe localized itching and low-grade fever only
options.B: Petechiae, respiratory distress, and altered mental status
options.C: Rapid bone healing and excessive calcium deposition
options.D: Complete paralysis restricted exclusively to the facial muscles

explanation: Fat embolism syndrome typically presents with a classic triad of petechiae (pinpoint rashes), respiratory distress, and neurological changes like altered mental status. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h8)

question: What is the term for a fracture that fails to heal properly despite adequate treatment over a prolonged period?
explanation: Non-union occurs when the bone fails to heal and form a solid bony bridge even after an extended period of time. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h8)

question: Which dietary components are especially important to encourage in patients recovering from a fracture to support bone mineralization?

options.A: High amounts of simple sugars and sodium
options.B: Protein, calcium, vitamin C, and vitamin D
options.C: Strictly saturated fats and refined starches
options.D: High levels of carbonated beverages and caffeine

explanation: A diet rich in protein, calcium, vitamin C, and vitamin D provides the essential building blocks for collagen synthesis and bone tissue repair. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h9)

question: What is a primary goal of incorporating early rehabilitation into the nursing care plan for fracture recovery?

options.A: To keep the patient on strict bed rest for at least six months
options.B: To restore joint range of motion, muscle strength, and functional independence
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for any pain medication
options.D: To induce intentional non-union of the fracture site

explanation: Early rehabilitation works to safely restore joint range of motion, rebuild muscle strength, and help the patient regain functional independence. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h9)
